identity.notes: The address type (public or random) is not recorded. Upstream keys reconnects on the platform's peripheral identifier (a CoreBluetooth UUID on macOS), which is stable for a bonded device on that host. If the address turns out to rotate, the bond's identity key resolves it on a bonded host. A host that has never bonded should then key on the local name instead.

methods.notes: The upstream client scans for about 10 s and keeps any result whose name starts with either prefix. The scanner advertises only while it has power from the diagnostic connector, which usually means the ignition must be on. A BGX13P peripheral takes one central at a time, and the vendor warns that a previously paired phone nearby can reconnect on its own. A scanner held by that phone is not available, and a connected BLE peripheral usually stops advertising (see pairing.exclusivity).

host_compatibility.basis: The vendor's own iOS app, and the upstream Bleak client, which its author ran on macOS (Bleak's CoreBluetooth backend): scan, bond, initialise and poll all worked there.
host_compatibility.notes: Pairing happens implicitly, on the read of the encrypted characteristic. The bond then appears in the macOS Bluetooth device list.

host_compatibility.basis: The vendor's Android app, supported on Android 8.0 and later per the vendor's compatibility article. No third-party Android client is known.
host_compatibility.notes: The vendor warns that many aftermarket Android head units run a common ROM that blocks the scanner from pairing, and knows of no workaround. That is a property of those ROMs, not of the Android stack in general.

identification.notes: Name only. The BGX Xpress Streaming service UUID (331a36f5-2459-45ea-9d95-6142f0c4b307) is inferred, not observed, and nothing records whether this product advertises it. It would also match every other BGX13P product, so it is deliberately not an identification axis. The source does not say which LE hardware line advertises which prefix. LSB2 is the vendor's model code for the BlueDriver Bluetooth Pro (the CERT note and the LSB2 owner's guide both use it), so "LSB2-" is presumably the model code plus a per-unit suffix. No suffix is recorded.

device.name: BlueDriver Bluetooth Pro OBD-II Scan Tool (Bluetooth LE)
device.notes:
A plug-in OBD-II scanner sold with a vendor phone app. This spec covers the Bluetooth LE scanners, which advertise a local name starting "BlueDriv" or "LSB2-". Per the vendor, these units have "LE" engraved on the side, or are the BlueDriver Pro Next-Gen, which is always LE. The original Bluetooth Classic BlueDriver (no "LE" marking, paired from the phone's Bluetooth settings) is a different radio path. It has not been researched and nothing here describes it.
EVIDENCE BASE: the open project sjalkote/bluedriver-reverse-engineering (README.md and main.py, pinned in `evidence`) was built from Apple PacketLogger HCI logs of the BlueDriver iOS app while it paired and streamed live data. The author then replicated the session in a Python Bleak client that connects, bonds, initialises and polls PIDs. The repository has no licence, so this spec restates its facts in its own words and tables and copies none of its code. Silicon Labs' BGX13P documentation supplies the service UUID and the reading of the flow-control bytes. Vendor support articles supply the pairing window, the LED meanings and the fact that firmware updates exist. This project holds no capture of its own and has driven no hardware.
STACK: the phone talks to a Silicon Labs BGX13P module over its Xpress Streaming service. Behind it sits an ELM327-style OBD core that implements the vendor's "LM" commands and the OBD-II protocols. Upstream says the LM commands are handled by the BGX overlay rather than the ELM core; which chip actually parses them is not established. Four application rules sit on top of the stock BGX profile, and a client that misses any one of them gets nothing useful back:
  1. Every stream byte is XORed with 0x26, except that 0x0D (CR) and
     0x3E ('>') pass through unchanged (protocol_details.wire_codec).
  2. The client announces a receive window on DATA (00 ff 7f) and must
     acknowledge every DATA notification with 01 <len> 00. Without the
     acknowledgement the scanner stops after the first fragment.
  3. A fixed nine-command LM init has to run before any PID query works
     (`initialization`).
  4. After the init, standard ELM327 AT commands must not be sent. ATZ,
     ATE0 and the rest corrupt the firmware's state, and every later
     query answers NO DATA. Upstream gives no recovery. Unplugging the
     scanner to power-cycle it is the obvious remedy, but it is untested.

Generic ELM327 behaviour (prompt handling, protocol numbers, the AT vocabulary) is documented in obd2-bluetooth-adapter. PID formulas are in the obd2-pid-reference spec. This spec records only what BlueDriver does differently.
WHY THE PAIRING WINDOW EXISTS: CERT/CC VU#615456 (CVE-2016-2354, April 2016) found that the "BlueDriver LSB2" took Bluetooth connections with no PIN, so anyone in radio range could reach the vehicle's diagnostic bus. The vendor's fix was a firmware update that limits discoverability to one minute after the scanner is plugged in, which is the 60-second window in `pairing`. The note does not say which radio that 2016 unit used. The LE units covered here already ship with the window, so this spec records the note as history rather than as a `security_advisory`. Just Works still means that whoever can plug the scanner in can pair with it.
OUT OF SCOPE: the vendor app's enhanced and manufacturer diagnostics (ABS/SRS/TPMS and similar), repair reports and every cloud feature. Also firmware update (only its existence is recorded, under `features`) and DTC clearing (mode 04), which the source never exercised.
SAFETY: reading PIDs is diagnostic only and moves nothing. Two practical hazards remain. OBD pin 16 is usually unswitched, so a scanner left in the connector draws on the battery. And a live-data display must not be read by the driver while the vehicle is moving.

openness.notes: Two layers with different provenance. The BLE transport matches a stock Silicon Labs BGX13P "Bluetooth Xpress" module, whose GATT profile and flow control Silicon Labs documents publicly. The application layer is the vendor's own and undocumented: the XOR wire encoding, the LM command set and the way the ELM327-style core is configured. Everything known about it comes from one open project's HCI captures.

upstream_docs.covers: The radio module's layer only: the Xpress Streaming service, its three characteristics (the same UUIDs as CMD, DATA and STATUS here), the three-byte Fast-Ack streaming control messages, and the Mode values. It says nothing about BlueDriver's XOR encoding, its LM commands or its OBD behaviour.
upstream_docs.title: Silicon Labs BGX: BLE Services

upstream_docs.covers: The module family's pairing and bonding behaviour: Just Works or passkey, and a bond table of up to 14 hosts with least-recently-used eviction. These are module defaults, not confirmed product settings.
upstream_docs.title: Silicon Labs BGX: Security

enter_pairing_mode.indicator: No distinct pairing indicator. The LED is solid blue at power-up, then flashes red (BlueDriver Pro) or turns green (Pro Next-Gen) while it waits for an app. It flashes blue once a phone is connected and talking to it.
enter_pairing_mode.notes: Whether a host that has already bonded can reconnect outside the window is not stated by any source. CERT's wording ("discoverability") leaves open whether the scanner stops advertising after the minute or only stops accepting new pairings. The stock BGX13P can do the latter: with pairing turned off, bonded hosts still connect. Upstream reconnects straight to a known address, and the vendor's advice for a bonded phone that will not connect is again to unplug and replug.

procedures.basis: Vendor support articles "Device Not Pairing - Device type LE engraved on device" and "Android Troubleshooting" (60-second window, restarted by unplugging and replugging). CERT/CC VU#615456 records the origin: the 2016 firmware fix for CVE-2016-2354 limited discoverability to one minute after plug-in, and only after plug-in, not at every ignition-on. Upstream's instructions to connect right after plugging in are consistent with this. Not replayed here.
procedures.description: The scanner is pairable for about a minute after it powers up from the connector. If the window passes, unplug the scanner and plug it back in to reopen it.
procedures.name: Plug the scanner in with the ignition on, then pair within 60 seconds

steps.action: Turn the ignition on and plug the scanner into the diagnostic connector (unplug it first if it is already in).
Connect and read the encrypted characteristic 12e868e7-c926-4906-96c8-a7ee81d4b1b3 before 60 seconds have passed.
steps.expect: The host completes LE Secure Connections Just Works pairing with no prompt and stores the bond.

exclusivity.notes: One central at a time. A BGX13P peripheral accepts a single connection (Silicon Labs), and the vendor's troubleshooting assumes another phone can take it. More than one host stays bonded: the vendor text implies it, and a stock BGX13P keeps 14 bonds. So adding a client does not unbind the phone app. It just has to lose the race for the connection.
exclusivity.recovery: Fully close the vendor app, including in the background. Turn Bluetooth off on every other phone or tablet that has paired with the scanner, because the vendor says they reconnect by themselves. Then unplug and replug the scanner and connect within 60 seconds.

pairing.notes: Pairing is plain LE link-layer security with nothing above it. The scanner answers the SMP Pairing Request with IO capability NoInputNoOutput. Whatever the host offers, that forces LE Secure Connections Just Works, with no PIN and no confirmation dialog. CoreBluetooth has no pairing call of its own, so the vendor app triggers pairing by reading the encrypted characteristic 12e868e7-c926-4906-96c8-a7ee81d4b1b3, and upstream does the same. On later connections the same read simply runs on the already-encrypted link, or fails harmlessly if the bond is cached. Silicon Labs documents the stock BGX streaming service as always requiring an encrypted link, so the XOR layer is obfuscation on top of real link encryption, not a replacement for it. `bonding: required` reflects that the bond is persisted and reused (macOS lists the scanner as a saved device after one run upstream) and that a host without one can only pair inside the 60 s window. Whether the scanner refuses a pairing request that does not set the bonding flag is not established.

unpair.notes: No scanner-side unpair is documented. On the host side, forget the scanner in the OS Bluetooth settings. The vendor says to do exactly that when a bonded iPhone will not reconnect. On the scanner side, bonds presumably age out through the BGX module's 14-entry least-recently-used table (a module default, not confirmed).

issued_to_client: The LE bond (long-term key), held by the host operating system's Bluetooth stack rather than by the application
credentials.notes: No application-layer credential exists. The XOR 0x26 encoding is a fixed obfuscation shared by every unit, not a key. Link security is LE Secure Connections Just Works. That gives encryption but no protection against a man in the middle, and anyone who plugs the scanner in can pair a phone inside the window.
stored_on_device: LE bond keys for each host that has paired (up to 14 on a stock BGX13P; not confirmed for this product)

factory_reset.description: Unplugging the scanner is a power cycle, not a reset. It restarts the 60 s pairing window and presumably clears the firmware state that stray AT commands corrupt, but no source says it drops bonds. On the stock BGX13P the bond table holds 14 hosts and evicts the least recently used one when a new host bonds. If this product keeps that default, old bonds age out on their own. That is a module default, not a product fact.
factory_reset.effect: None is documented. The vendor's support pages describe no reset for the scanner itself. Their remedies are all on the phone side: forget the device, clear the app's data, or unplug and replug. The scanner stores no user configuration a client sets. The only state it is known to hold is its bonds with paired hosts, and whether anything short of eviction clears those is not established.

methods.description: Plug in with the ignition on, find the scanner by name, connect, and read the encrypted characteristic. On first contact that makes the host pair (Just Works, no PIN) and store a bond. Then open the DATA receive window, run the nine-command LM init, and poll mode-01 PIDs one at a time. No button, no PIN and no account are involved.

steps.action: Turn the ignition on (engine running, or key-on/engine-off), then plug the scanner into the diagnostic connector.
steps.expect: LED solid blue while the scanner starts, then flashing red (BlueDriver Pro) or green (Pro Next-Gen). Either means it is powered and talking to the vehicle but no app is connected yet.

steps.action: Within 60 seconds of plugging in, scan for a local name starting with 'BlueDriv' or 'LSB2-' and connect.
steps.notes: 60 s is the vendor's pairing window for a phone that has not bonded yet. Unplugging and replugging restarts it.

steps.action: Run the connection handshake in `initialization`. Its read of the encrypted characteristic makes the host pair on first contact.
steps.expect: The host stores a bond. Each LM init command's reply ends with the '>' prompt, and LMDP answers with the detected OBD protocol number.

steps.action: Poll mode-01 PIDs one request at a time, waiting for '>' before each next write.
steps.expect: Space-separated hex data bytes, then CR and '>' (see payload_formats.ElmResponse).

timing.notes: All values are from upstream. The timeouts (3 s per init reply, 20 s for the pairing read) are the upstream client's own choices, not device limits. The per-query figures and the roughly 15 ms connection interval were observed in its captures.

causes: The DATA notification was not acknowledged. Write 01 <len> 00 to DATA for every fragment, immediately, before decoding it.
The 00 ff 7f receive-window message was never written to DATA before the first command.
troubleshooting.symptom: The first reply fragment arrives, then nothing; the '>' prompt never comes.

causes: A standard AT command (ATZ, ATE0, ATSP, ...) was sent after the LM init. That breaks the firmware's state. No recovery is documented. Unplugging the scanner, reconnecting and rerunning the init without AT commands is the obvious thing to try (untested).
The LM init was skipped or run out of order.
ATRV and ATDP answer NO DATA by design. Use PID 0142 for voltage and LMDP for the protocol.
A new command was written before the previous reply's '>' arrived. There is no pipelining: any new input makes the ELM core abort the query in flight.
troubleshooting.symptom: Queries time out at random, or replies are cut short.

causes: The scanner is in LMX1 (exhaustive timing, ~200 ms per query). Send LMX0 for live polling.
troubleshooting.symptom: Live data refreshes about once a second.

causes: More than 60 s passed since plug-in on a host that has not bonded. Unplug, replug and connect promptly.
Another phone that paired earlier, or the vendor app running in the background, already holds the scanner's only connection. Close the app and turn Bluetooth off on the other devices.
The ignition is off, so the scanner has no power.
The host kept a stale bond. Forget the scanner in the OS Bluetooth settings and pair again inside the 60 s window.
troubleshooting.symptom: The scanner is not found, or the pairing read times out.

causes: The scanner is in firmware recovery mode after an interrupted update. Only the vendor app's update flow recovers it (see features.firmware_update).
troubleshooting.symptom: The LED is solid red as soon as the scanner is plugged in.

setup.notes: Nothing to provision: there is no Wi-Fi, and the documented path needs no account. The vendor app offers an account or a guest mode, and per the vendor all local diagnostics work offline. The only one-time act is the LE bond described in `pairing`, and it must be made within 60 seconds of plugging the scanner in. After that, every connection runs the handshake in top-level `initialization`. Confidence is medium because there is a working open client (upstream) and vendor support articles, but nothing has been replayed here.

rejoin.notes: Moving to a new phone or client is just pairing again inside the 60 s window after plug-in. A phone that bonded earlier may reconnect first and take the only connection. Turn Bluetooth off on it, or forget the scanner there, before pairing the new one.

evidence.open_questions: The service UUID and every BGX field name are inferences from the module documentation, not observations. The biggest open point is the flow control. Under the BGX reading, 00 ff 7f announces 32767 bytes of client buffer, and a peripheral honouring that should not need an acknowledgement per fragment. Yet upstream saw the scanner stall after one fragment without them. Either this firmware treats the window differently or something else is at work. A capture that withholds the acknowledgements and watches the stall would settle it. Until then, do what the vendor app does and acknowledge every fragment.
evidence.public_reporting: CERT/CC Vulnerability Note VU#615456 (CVE-2016-2354, 2016-04-07, revised 2016-04-20), read 2026-09-28. It names the "BlueDriver LSB2", describes Bluetooth access with no PIN, and gives the vendor's fix: firmware that limits discoverability to one minute after plug-in. That is the only source for why the 60-second window exists.
evidence.public_research: sjalkote/bluedriver-reverse-engineering, read at commit b4d1bc1 (master, 2026-09). README.md gives the name prefixes, the four characteristics and their properties, the SMP IO capability, the XOR key and its two pass-through bytes, the 00 ff 07 / 01 01 00 / 00 ff 7f / 01 <len> 00 byte sequences, the LM init order with its expected replies, the LMX0 and LMX1 timings, the AT-command and ATRV/ATDP pitfalls, the tested PID table and the multi-PID and no-pipelining findings. main.py is a working Bleak client that confirms the order of operations: subscribe, pairing read, Device Information reads, window, init, then polling. It also gives the upstream timeouts and the reply parser's handling of error words, frame markers and optional 41 echoes. Its facts are restated in this spec's own words; none of its code is copied (the repository carries no licence).
evidence.vendor_documentation: Silicon Labs BGX documentation (BLE Services and Security pages, read 2026-09-28). It establishes that the three streaming characteristic UUIDs here are the stock BGX Xpress Streaming Rx, Tx and Mode characteristics, and gives their service UUID. It defines the three-byte Fast-Ack streaming control messages that 00 ff 07, 00 ff 7f and 01 <len> 00 fit, the Mode values, the single-central limit, and the 14-bond table. BlueDriver support articles (read 2026-09-28) give the LE and Classic hardware split, the in-app pairing flow with its 60-second window, the LED meanings, the firmware recovery mode, and the offline scope of diagnostics. The LSB2 owner's guide names the model and the app's "Update Sensor F/W" entry but says nothing about pairing or the radio.

dfu_mode.notes: In firmware recovery mode the LED is solid red from the moment the scanner is plugged in, and it cannot be connected to normally. Its advertised name and services in that state are not recorded.

enter.notes: How the app starts an update is not documented, and no command is declared here. The stock BGX13P module family also has its own Silicon Labs OTA path, which per the module datasheet accepts only images Silicon Labs has signed and encrypted. Whether this product exposes it, or updates the OBD core some other way, is not recorded.

image.notes: The vendor says downloading firmware updates needs an internet connection, so images come from the vendor's servers through the app. Format and signing are not known.

dfu.notes: Recorded so the standing question has an answer: the scanner does take firmware updates, delivered by the vendor app over BLE. Everything about how is outside the researched scope. A third-party client should never attempt one.

recovery.notes: Per the vendor, an update interrupted by a phone disconnect or power loss leaves the scanner in recovery mode (solid red LED). Running the app's firmware update again reinstalls the firmware.

initialization.notes: Subscribe CMD first. The scanner answers with a 00 ff 07 notification (BGX Initial Buffer Size, 2047 bytes). Later CMD notifications (01 01 00 after each command) can be ignored by a client that sends one command at a time.
Subscribe DATA; every reply arrives here.
Subscribe STATUS, as upstream does; its bursts are not decoded (see the characteristic's notes). Never write to it.

Read the encrypted characteristic. On a host that has not bonded, this starts SMP pairing, which completes as LE Secure Connections Just Works with no user interaction. It must happen within 60 s of plug-in (see device.pairing). On a bonded host it just reads over the encrypted link. Upstream allows 20 s, and if the read errors it assumes a cached bond and continues after a 0.5 s pause. What the returned value means is not documented, so do not depend on it. The characteristic's service is not recorded, so look it up by characteristic UUID (it is not one of the three BGX streaming characteristics). If a host stack refuses the three subscriptions above with an insufficient-encryption error instead of pairing on its own, do this read first and then subscribe (hypothesis; upstream's order was run only on macOS).
Optional: firmware revision string, for display only.
Optional: model number string, for display only.
Open the receive window (DATA command open_receive_window). Not XOR-encoded.

initialization.description: From here on, for EVERY DATA notification: immediately write 01 <len> 00 to DATA (the ack_fragment command, <len> = that notification's byte count), then XOR-decode the fragment and append it to the reply buffer. A reply is complete when the decoded buffer contains '>'. Every LM step below must wait for that prompt before the next write. This is receive logic that no fixed byte sequence can state, so a client has to implement it itself. A consumer that cannot must stop here: without the acknowledgements the scanner stalls after the first fragment.

initialization.notes: LMI. Wait for '>' first (upstream allows 3 s), then pause 50 ms. Reply: '?' or 'OSAPI v2.60' CR 'OK'.
LML0. Wait for '>' first. Reply: '?' (expected; the vendor app sends it regardless).
LMI (second). Wait for '>' first. Reply: 'OSAPI v2.60' CR 'OK'.
LMDP. Wait for '>' first. Reply: the detected protocol number (protocol_details.lmdp_protocol_numbers) CR 'OK'.
LMI (third). Wait for '>' first. Reply: 'OSAPI v2.60' CR 'OK'.
LMX1 (exhaustive timing). Wait for '>' first. Reply: 'OK'.

LMX0 (fast timing). Wait for '>' first. Reply: 'OK'. The init is now complete. The ELM core is left with echo off, headers off, linefeeds off, spaces on and automatic protocol selection. Mode-01 PIDs now work raw. Send no AT commands from here on.

known_limitations:
No capability class is claimed. The core behaves like an ELM327 for mode-01 reads, but the AT command set is off-limits after the mandatory LM init: any AT command corrupts the firmware state and every later query returns NO DATA. So nothing that needs AT configuration (custom headers, protocol forcing, raw frames, flow control, monitor mode) is available to a third-party client. This is a firmware restriction, not a sign of clone silicon.
multiframe_rx rests on the six-PID mode-01 request, which CAN vehicles answer in one multi-frame response. Non-CAN protocols do not support combined requests.
ATRV (adapter voltage) and ATDP (protocol name) answer NO DATA. Use PID 0142 for voltage and LMDP for the protocol number.
One query at a time. A command written while a query is in flight aborts it.
Mode 03 (read DTCs), mode 04 (clear DTCs) and the vendor's enhanced manufacturer diagnostics were not exercised by the source and are not documented here.

requests.description: Mode 01 PID 00. Listed by upstream as a common PID but not among the ones it tested.
requests.name: read_supported_pids
requests.notes: Reply carries data bytes only (no 41 00 echo) on this scanner; see payload_formats.ElmResponse.

requests.description: Mode 01 PID 0C, the upstream worked example (reply '0F 80' = 992 rpm).
requests.name: read_engine_rpm

requests.description: Mode 01 PID 42, the stand-in for battery voltage because ATRV is unavailable.
requests.name: read_module_voltage

requests.description: One mode-01 request carrying six PIDs (0C 0D 05 04 11 0B). CAN only.
requests.name: read_live_six_pids

ElmResponse.description: One reply from the ELM core as it appears on DATA after XOR-decoding the concatenated fragments. The LM init leaves the core with echo off, headers off, linefeeds off and spaces on, so a reply is space-separated hex text, then CR, then the '>' prompt. Every character except CR and '>' is XOR-encoded on the wire.
parse_rules: Acknowledge each DATA notification (01 <len> 00) before anything else, then XOR-decode it: every byte b becomes b ^ 0x26, except 0x0d and 0x3e, which stay as they are.
Append decoded fragments to a buffer that was cleared before the command was sent. The reply is complete when the buffer contains '>'. Do not parse earlier; replies commonly span two notifications.
Drop the '>' and treat CR as a separator. Lines are CR-only (linefeeds are off).
If the text contains NO DATA, UNABLE, ERROR, STOPPED, SEARCHING or a bare '?', the query produced no value. These are standard ELM327 status words; see obd2-bluetooth-adapter.
LM commands answer with text lines followed by OK (e.g. 'OSAPI v2.60' then 'OK'; for LMDP, the protocol number then 'OK'). The first token of an LMDP reply is the protocol number.

Single-PID mode-01 reply: per upstream, ONLY the data bytes, with no 41 mode byte and no PID echo. Upstream's example for 010C is '0F 80' followed by CR and '>'. Strip a leading '41 <pid>' defensively in case a firmware revision restores the echo, as upstream's parser does.

Multi-PID mode-01 reply (CAN only): each requested PID number comes back ahead of its own data bytes, with no leading 41. Upstream's parser also skips a leading 41 if one appears. CAN multi-frame output can carry ELM frame-index tokens ending in ':' ('0:', '1:'); drop those, join the remaining hex, and walk it PID by PID using each PID's data length from obd2-pid-reference. If the walk hits a byte that is not the next expected PID, the scanner returned fewer PIDs; fall back to single-PID requests.
Decode data bytes with the J1979 formulas in obd2-pid-reference (the nine upstream tested are tabulated in protocol_details.tested_pids).

StreamControlMessage.description: The three-byte BGX Fast-Ack flow-control message. The scanner sends it as a CMD notification, and the client writes it to DATA without response. It is never XOR-encoded. The field meanings come from Silicon Labs' BGX documentation, and the four instances below match that layout. Upstream describes the same bytes without naming the fields.

fields.description: 0x00 = Initial Buffer Size; 0x01 = Buffer Bytes Freed.
fields.name: opcode

fields.description: Bytes 1-2, unsigned 16-bit little-endian: the buffer size (opcode 0x00) or the number of bytes freed (opcode 0x01).
fields.name: byte_count

values.00 ff 07: scanner -> client on CMD at connect: Initial Buffer Size 2047 bytes
values.00 ff 7f: client -> scanner on DATA before the first command: Initial Buffer Size 32767 bytes (upstream: 'a 255-byte credit window')
values.01 01 00: scanner -> client on CMD after each command: Buffer Bytes Freed 1 (upstream: 'ACK')
values.01 <len> 00: client -> scanner on DATA for every DATA notification: Buffer Bytes Freed <len>

encrypted_characteristic.role: Pairing trigger. Reading it on a host with no bond makes the stack run SMP, which completes as LE Secure Connections Just Works (the scanner advertises IO capability NoInputNoOutput). It is not one of the BGX streaming characteristics. What its value means is not documented.

after_init: Mode-01 PIDs are sent raw (e.g. 010C + CR). No further setup is needed.
Never send AT commands. ATZ, ATE0 and the rest corrupt the firmware's state and every query returns NO DATA.
ATRV and ATDP return NO DATA. Use PID 0142 and LMDP instead.
LMX1 and LMX0 can be switched at any time. The vendor app uses LMX1 only for its one-time monitor and freeze-frame scans, and LMX0 for live data.
lm_init.description: The vendor app's mandatory initialisation, in order, sent over CMD after the 00 ff 7f window message on DATA. Wait for '>' after each command. The expected replies are upstream's table.
lm_init.example_version_string: OSAPI v2.60 (the product firmware string in LMI replies, as captured upstream)
lm_init.resulting_elm_state: echo off, headers off, linefeeds off, spaces on, automatic protocol selection

sequence.role: fast timing (~45 ms per query); leaves the scanner ready for live polling

lmdp_protocol_numbers.description: LMDP reply values. They are the ELM327 protocol numbers (see obd2-bluetooth-adapter).

multi_pid_requests.pipelining: not supported: a command written while a query is in flight aborts that query
multi_pid_requests.protocols: ISO 15765-4 (CAN) only; non-CAN vehicles answer incompletely, so fall back to one PID per request
multi_pid_requests.reply_layout: each PID number, then its data bytes, repeated; no leading 41 (see payload_formats.ElmResponse)

tested_pids.description: The mode-01 PIDs upstream ran against a vehicle through this scanner. Data bytes are A, B in reply order, and multi-byte values are big-endian as J1979 defines them. The formulas agree with the obd2-pid-reference spec, which is authoritative for these and every other PID.

timing.notes: All observed by upstream. Serial polling at 40-50 ms per PID matched the vendor iOS app's refresh rate. The combined six-PID request costs one round trip instead of six.

caveats:
The mapping is not one-to-one, so two plaintext bytes cannot be represented. '+' (0x2b) encodes to 0x0d and 0x18 encodes to 0x3e, so both would decode as CR and '>'. Neither appears in ELM327 command or reply text, so the collision does not arise in practice. It is arithmetic from the rule above, not an observation.
CR is the command terminator, and '>' is the end-of-reply prompt. Both survive the encoding, so a receiver can find the end of a reply on the raw wire bytes without decoding them first.
wire_codec.description: Obfuscation applied by the BlueDriver firmware to every stream byte on CMD writes and DATA notifications, in both directions. It does not apply to the three-byte stream control messages, which travel as-is.
wire_codec.rule: wire = plain ^ 0x26 for every byte, except 0x0d (CR) and 0x3e ('>'), which are sent unchanged. Decoding applies the same rule to the wire bytes.

remaining_unknowns: The primary service UUID is not stated by the source. 331a36f5-2459-45ea-9d95-6142f0c4b307 is inferred from Silicon Labs' BGX documentation and has not been seen in a BlueDriver GATT dump.
Which service holds the ENCRYPTED characteristic 12e868e7-c926-4906-96c8-a7ee81d4b1b3, and what the value it returns means.
What the STATUS (BGX Mode) bursts carry. The BGX mode values 1/2/3 are a hypothesis.
Why the scanner needs an acknowledgement for every DATA fragment when the window it was given (00 ff 7f) reads as 32767 bytes under the BGX layout.
The meaning of LMD and LML0, and why the vendor app sends LML0 when its expected answer is '?'. Also whether LMI's first-call '?' carries any meaning.
Whether the LM commands are handled by the BGX13P module or by the OBD core behind it.

Whether the BlueDriver Pro (LE, engraved 'LE') and the Pro Next-Gen share this stack, and which of the two advertises 'BlueDriv' and which 'LSB2-'. The upstream author does not say which unit they had.
The older Bluetooth Classic BlueDriver was not researched. Which radio the 2016 LSB2 in CERT VU#615456 used, and whether the Classic and LE units share the LSB2 model code, is not established.

Whether a host that is already bonded can connect outside the 60-second pairing window (CERT VU#615456 says only that discoverability ends after one minute), and whether the scanner refuses a pairing request without the bonding flag.
The scanner's BLE address type (public or random) and the format of the 'LSB2-' suffix.

Mode 02 (freeze frame), 03 (read DTCs), 06, 09 and the vendor's enhanced diagnostics were not documented. Mode 04 (clear DTCs) was never exercised. It erases stored codes and resets readiness monitors, so a client that adds it should treat it as advanced and confirm first.
How firmware updates are delivered, whether images are signed, and how the scanner advertises in recovery mode.
The Device Information strings' actual values, and whether the firmware revision string is the BGX module's or the product's.

lm_d.description: LMD + CR. Part of the LM init (sent twice). Replies OK. Its meaning is not known.

lm_identify.description: LMI + CR. Firmware identity probe. The first call of the init may answer "?". The others answer with an OSAPI version line and OK (e.g. "OSAPI v2.60", CR, "OK", CR, ">"). Sent three times during the LM init.

lm_l0.description: LML0 + CR. Part of the LM init. The expected reply is "?" (the ELM core's unknown-command answer), and the vendor app sends it anyway. Its meaning is not known.

lm_protocol.description: LMDP + CR. Reports the OBD protocol the scanner auto-detected, as one ELM-style protocol number (0-9 or A, table in protocol_details.lmdp_protocol_numbers), then CR, OK, CR, '>'. Use this in place of ATDP, which answers NO DATA here.

lm_timing_exhaustive.description: LMX1 + CR. Exhaustive response timing: the firmware waits out its full ~200 ms timeout on every query, whether or not the ECU has answered. The vendor app switches to this for its one-time monitor and freeze-frame scans. Replies OK.

lm_timing_fast.description: LMX0 + CR. Fast response timing: the reply comes back as soon as the ECU answers, about 45 ms per query. This is the last command of the LM init and the mode for live polling. Replies OK.

read_coolant_temperature.description: 0105 + CR. Engine coolant temperature: 1 data byte A, C = A - 40.

read_engine_load.description: 0104 + CR. Calculated engine load: 1 data byte A, % = A * 100 / 255.

read_engine_rpm.description: 010C + CR. Engine speed: 2 data bytes A B, rpm = (A*256 + B) / 4 (unsigned 16-bit big-endian, scale 0.25). Upstream's example reply is "0F 80" plus CR and '>', which decodes to 992 rpm.

read_fuel_level.description: 012F + CR. Fuel tank level input: 1 data byte A, % = A * 100 / 255.

read_intake_air_temperature.description: 010F + CR. Intake air temperature: 1 data byte A, C = A - 40.

read_intake_manifold_pressure.description: 010B + CR. Intake manifold absolute pressure: 1 data byte A, kPa = A.

read_live_six_pids.description: 010C0D0504110B + CR. One mode-01 request for six PIDs (rpm, speed, coolant, load, throttle, manifold pressure), the most one request may carry. CAN vehicles only. The reply echoes each PID number before its data bytes (layout in payload_formats.ElmResponse). If fewer than the six PIDs come back (non-CAN protocols), fall back to one PID per request. Costs one BLE round trip instead of six.

read_module_voltage.description: 0142 + CR. Control module voltage: 2 data bytes A B, V = (A*256 + B) / 1000 (unsigned 16-bit big-endian, scale 0.001). This stands in for battery voltage, because ATRV answers NO DATA on this scanner.

read_supported_pids.description: 0100 + CR. Mode 01 PID 00, the supported-PID bitmap for PIDs 01-20 (4 data bytes, bitmask per obd2-pid-reference). Upstream lists it among common PIDs but not among the ones it tested.

read_throttle_position.description: 0111 + CR. Throttle position: 1 data byte A, % = A * 100 / 255.

read_vehicle_speed.description: 010D + CR. Vehicle speed: 1 data byte A, km/h = A.

characteristics.name: CMD (BGX Peripheral Receive, Rx)
characteristics.notes: Client to scanner: XOR-encoded ASCII commands, each ending in CR (0x0D, which passes through the encoding unchanged). The upstream client writes without response. Scanner to client: notifications here are BGX streaming control messages, not data. On the initial connection the scanner sends 00 ff 07. The BGX procedure has a peripheral send this when the central enables notifications here. Upstream calls this a status message; the BGX layout reads it as Initial Buffer Size, 0x07ff = 2047 bytes. After each command it sends 01 01 00, which upstream calls an ACK and the BGX layout reads as Buffer Bytes Freed = 1. Upstream ignores both and nothing breaks, because a single command of five to fifteen bytes never nears a 2047-byte window. The commands below are the exact wire bytes, already XOR-encoded. Each description gives the plaintext. Send one command, then wait for the '>' prompt on DATA before sending the next.

ack_fragment.description: 01 <len> 00: acknowledge one DATA notification. <len> is the exact byte count of the fragment being acknowledged, as a 16-bit little-endian value. A fragment never exceeds 250 bytes, so on the wire this is always 01, the length, then 00. BGX Fast-Ack names it Buffer Bytes Freed (opcode 0x01). Send one per notification, as soon as it arrives.

packet_layout.0: opcode 0x01: Buffer Bytes Freed (BGX Fast-Ack naming)
packet_layout.2: fragment length, high byte (always 0x00 for a BLE fragment)

bytes_freed.description: Byte count of the DATA notification being acknowledged, as received (before XOR decoding, which does not change the length). The 250 ceiling is the BGX characteristic's maximum value length.

open_receive_window.description: 00 ff 7f, written once per connection after subscribing and before the first CMD write. Upstream calls it opening a 255-byte receive credit window. Under the BGX Fast-Ack layout it is an Initial Buffer Size message (opcode 0x00) announcing 0x7fff = 32767 bytes of client buffer. The bytes are the same whichever reading is right. Upstream pauses about 100 ms after writing it.

packet_layout.0: opcode 0x00: Initial Buffer Size (BGX Fast-Ack naming)
packet_layout.2: buffer size, high byte (0x7f); little-endian 0x7fff = 32767 bytes

characteristics.name: DATA (BGX Peripheral Transmit, Tx)
characteristics.notes: Scanner to client: XOR-encoded reply fragments from the ELM core. One reply commonly spans two notifications, so decode each fragment and append it to a buffer until the decoded buffer contains '>'. Clear the buffer before each new command, so a stale '>' cannot end the next wait early. Client to scanner: only the three-byte stream control messages below, written without response and NOT XOR-encoded. Acknowledge every notification, immediately and before decoding it. Upstream found that without these acknowledgements the scanner stops after the first fragment.

characteristics.name: STATUS (BGX Stream Mode, Mode)
characteristics.notes: Upstream subscribes and logs occasional "status bursts" here but never decoded them. In the stock BGX profile this is the Mode characteristic. Its values are 1 = streaming, 2 = local command mode, 3 = remote command mode, so the bursts are plausibly mode reports (hypothesis). Silicon Labs also lists write-without-response for it; upstream did not report that property. Do NOT write it. On a BGX module a Mode write switches the module out of streaming, which would cut the OBD stream off. The upstream client never writes it, and the source records no write to it by the vendor app.

services.name: Silicon Labs BGX Xpress Streaming Service (inferred)
services.notes: INFERRED, not observed. Upstream lists the three characteristics below by UUID but never names their service. Silicon Labs' BGX documentation lists exactly these three characteristic UUIDs as the Xpress Streaming service 331a36f5-2459-45ea-9d95-6142f0c4b307, as Peripheral Receive (Rx), Peripheral Transmit (Tx) and Mode. The properties upstream observed match that table as well. No GATT dump of a BlueDriver confirms the service UUID, so a client should look the characteristics up by characteristic UUID across all services rather than depend on this one. The upstream names CMD / DATA / STATUS are kept, with the BGX names in each entry.

characteristics.name: Model Number String
characteristics.notes: ASCII/UTF-8 model string; length not recorded.

characteristics.name: Firmware Revision String
characteristics.notes: ASCII/UTF-8 firmware string; length not recorded. Whether it reports the BGX module's firmware or the product firmware (the LMI reply carries an "OSAPI" version) is not established.

services.name: Device Information
services.notes: Standard SIG service. Upstream reads the two strings below once after pairing, for display. The actual values seen are not recorded.
